questions.stem: Minutes after a user reports a suspicious email, a junior analyst notices the message has vanished from 40 mailboxes, the sender's domain is on the mail gateway blocklist, the user's laptop has been network-isolated by the EDR agent, and a ticket describing all of this is already open. options.text: A SIEM correlating related events into one alert
options.rationale: A SIEM detects and correlates events into alerts; it doesn't pull emails, block domains, or isolate hosts by itself.

options.text: A SOAR playbook acting through several tools
options.rationale: Correct: SOAR orchestrates the mail gateway, EDR, and ticketing tools and runs a predefined playbook, so the response happens without an analyst.

options.text: An IPS dropping malicious traffic inline by itself
options.rationale: An IPS can block traffic automatically, but inline on the network; it doesn't remove mail or open tickets across tools.

options.text: An attacker erasing evidence to hide the intrusion
options.rationale: Attacker cleanup wouldn't block the attacker's own domain, isolate the host, and document it in a ticket; these are defensive actions.

questions.explanation: SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) connects security tools and runs playbooks that act on detections, such as removing a phishing email, blocking the sender, and isolating the host. A SIEM detects and correlates; SOAR acts on what was detected.
questions.discriminator_tested: Coordinated actions across several tools with no analyst involved point to SOAR, while detection and correlation alone point to a SIEM.
